title: Long is the night (60–63)
hookLine: long is the night to the sleepless; the fool who knows he is a fool is wise so far

lines: THE LAST MILE OF THE HIKE.
cards: Three in the morning, wide awake, and the clock seems broken. Every time you check, it's been four minutes.
Or the last mile of a long hike, when your feet hurt and the trail keeps going, and that mile feels longer than the first five. Time stretches when things hurt.
The fifth chapter of the Dhammapada begins with exactly those two pictures, then adds a third that's much less comfortable.

teach.h: THE NIGHT, THE MILE, THE LIFE.
teach.b: Verse sixty, in Müller's English: “Long is the night to him who is awake; long is a mile to him who is tired; long is life to the foolish who do not know the true law.”
Two ordinary pictures, then the turn: life itself drags on, round after round, for someone who never sees how things really are.

teach.h: BALA — THE ONE WHO DOESN'T SEE.
teach.b: The chapter is called the fool, bala in Pali. The word also means a child, someone not grown up yet. It isn't about low intelligence.
It's about not seeing. Verse sixty-one says it's better to travel alone than with a fool.
Verse sixty-two describes one: my sons, my wealth, he thinks, and it torments him, though he doesn't even own himself, let alone his sons or his money.
Then verse sixty-three, and it's a gift: “The fool who knows his foolishness, is wise at least so far. But a fool who thinks himself wise, he is called a fool indeed.”
The commentary tells it with two pickpockets who went to hear the Buddha teach, planning to work the crowd. One started listening, and forgot to steal.
The teaching went in, and the story says he saw the truth right there. The other stole a coin and went home.
That evening, his wife mocked the first thief for coming home with nothing, calling him wise. The Buddha, hearing of it, spoke the verse. The one who knew he didn't know was the one who could learn.
There's real relief in that. You don't have to be wise to begin. You only have to notice where you aren't.

how: Buddhist teachers often quote verse sixty-three to encourage humility in study, and the story of the two pickpockets is a popular teaching tale.

o: a stubborn person who refuses all advice
someone with low intelligence or a weak mind
someone who doesn't see how things really are

games.q: match the pieces of verses sixty to sixty-three.

s: in the Dhammapada, 'fool' means someone of low intelligence
bala is someone who doesn't see how things are; the word also means a child.
verse sixty-three says the fool who knows his foolishness is wise so far
the one who thinks himself wise is the real fool.
verse sixty-two says the fool doesn't even own himself, let alone sons or wealth

games.q: you're a pickpocket in a crowd listening to the Buddha. the teaching starts to reach you. what does the story say happened?
o: you steal anyway; that's what you came for.
you listen, forget to steal, and see the truth.
you leave before it gets to you.
games.why: one thief listened and was changed; the other stole a coin. at home, the second thief's wife mocked the first as 'wise,' and the Buddha spoke verse sixty-three.

practice: With no shame at all, bring to mind one thing you don't really know but sometimes act as if you do: a topic you nod along to, a skill you bluff, something you've assumed about the people you love and never asked.
Just see it, like the first pickpocket, who forgot to steal because he started listening. Rest with the breath, and see whether admitting it puts down a small weight.

wordCard.voice: Bala. Fool, or child: the one who doesn't see, for whom the night is long, the mile is long, and life itself drags on; knowing it is already wise so far.

orig.note: Pali: fool, and also child: the title of chapter five.

carryVoice: Your line: wise so far. Knowing you don't know is where learning starts. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Long is the night to him who is awake; long is a mile to him who is tired; long is life to the foolish who do not know the true law.
The fool who knows his foolishness, is wise at least so far. But a fool who thinks himself wise, he is called a fool indeed.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 61–62; Dhammapada-atthakatha, story of the two pickpockets (verse 63)
